source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving (CogSci 2020)
finding: Describes MacGregor, Ormerod and Chronicle (2001) in the authors' own words. The progress criterion is a fixed ratio from the problem statement. For the nine-dot problem it is dots remaining over lines available. Insight comes at 'criterion failure': no move meets the criterion, so the solver widens the search. This is a binary trigger, not a felt gradual warmth.
numbers: No numbers for the 2001 paper itself. It names the criterion as 'the ratio of dots remaining to lines available'.
quote: insight occurs ... when 'criterion failure' arises, that is, when no further moves can be discovered that meet a criterion
limits: Secondary source (same lab). Does not give the 2001 nine-dot numbers. Competes with representational change theory.
agent_relevance: The best-supported human progress rule is a fixed, code-set criterion with a hard failure trigger. That is the same shape as our S6 count rule.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) CogSci 2020, matchstick algebra Experiments 1-2 (tests of progress cues)
finding: Cues to apparent progress change solution rates in matchstick algebra. High-value equations (a numeric signal pointing at the right move) were solved more often than low-value ones. Chunk tightness also mattered. Supports a progress-cue account alongside the knowledge account.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=121): low-value loose 77% (23/30), low-value tight 43% (13/30), high-value loose 90% (28/31), high-value tight 77% (24/31). Exp 2 (N=133) standard tautology: low-value 12% (4/32) vs high-value 62% (21/34); reverse tautology 72% (23/32) vs 77%. Logistic models chi2(3)=21.6 and 39.30, p<.001.
limits: Matchsticks, not nine-dot or eight-coin. Authors say CSPT does not explain initial difficulty; both knowledge and progress matter.
agent_relevance: Progress cues steer which move is tried first. A misleading progress signal can lock an agent into a wrong line, so a trigger must not rely on one cue.

source: Ormerod, Rusconi & Banks (2015) Modelling insight: the case of the nine-dot problem (ICCM 2015)
finding: ACT-R model of the nine-dot problem with a progress criterion. A first line is judged against: remaining dots divided by remaining lines. Relaxation of the minimisation heuristic is triggered by criterion failure. It reproduces impasse, fixation and rare solutions, and the 13-, 12- and 11-dot variant order. It reports that an internal first line leads to earlier criterion failure and more solutions (MacGregor 2001, Expts 4-5).
numbers: Model solution rate under 5% in 50 runs. 13-dot variant solved within 2 runs. 12- and 11-dot variants solved in under 10 runs. Internal vs external first line: significantly fewer runs for internal, p<.01 (quoted from MacGregor et al. 2001).
quote: Relaxation of minimisation is triggered by criterion failure.
limits: Model, not human data. Human numbers are second-hand from MacGregor et al. 2001. The original paper was not opened (publisher paywall).
agent_relevance: Shows the progress criterion can be written as code with a fixed threshold. Failure of the rule opens a wider search. A direct template for a no-progress trigger followed by a wider S6 search.

source: Spiridonov et al. (2019) The role of motor activity in insight problem solving (nine-dot): account of MacGregor et al. 2001
finding: Second-hand summary of MacGregor et al. (2001): a heuristic-search model with maximisation, progress monitoring and lookahead of 1 to 4 lines. Experiments 1-3 used simpler related problems that most people solved. Nobody solved the plain nine-dot in Exp 1.
numbers: MacGregor 2001 Exp 1 as reported here: 80 to 93% solved the simpler problems; no one solved the nine-dot problem. Lookahead depth 1 to 4 line segments.
limits: Second-hand. The 2001 paper's own tables were not read. Spiridonov argues motor activity matters, which the theory does not predict.
agent_relevance: Fills part of gap 2 only. The founding study showed a huge gap between easy variants and the nine-dot. The 2001 data are not clean support for a fixed criterion by themselves.

source: Ormerod, MacGregor & Chronicle (2002) Dynamics and constraints in insight problem solving, JEP:LMC 28, 791-799 (repository abstract)
finding: Two eight-coin experiments. Moves that look like progress but guarantee failure ('strategic moves') were predicted to attract solvers. Exp 1: solution rates were lower when such moves were available. Exp 2: people used visual hints about the correct first move less when such moves were available. Authors say insight needs both inappropriate constraints and a dynamic that steers search toward them.
numbers: No numbers on the repository page. Two experiments only.
limits: Abstract page only; full text not available. Rates, N and criterion numbers were not read.
agent_relevance: A visible-progress cue can pull a solver down a dead end. A progress signal can be wrong in a way that raises failure. Number-level claim still missing.

source: Ollinger, Jones, Faber & Knoblich (2013) Cognitive mechanisms of insight: heuristics and representational change in the eight-coin problem, JEP:LMC 39, 931-939 (abstract)
finding: Six new versions of the eight-coin problem. The earlier claim (Ormerod 2002) was that version differences come from the availability of progress-making moves in 2-D space. They find two other sources of difficulty: the assumption that the solution lies in 2-D space, and perceptual groupings. Move analysis showed people chose moves from their existing representation, not from good heuristics. Conclusion favours representational change theory.
numbers: 6 new versions; 2 difficulty sources. No participant numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only. A boundary condition on d05: the eight-coin data do not clearly support a fixed progress criterion.
agent_relevance: Progress monitoring is not the only story for stuck solvers. A representation-change operator may be needed beside a progress rule.

source: Smith & Kounios (1996) Sudden insight: all-or-none processing revealed by speed-accuracy decomposition, JEP:LMC 22, 1443-1462 (abstract page)
finding: Two experiments used speed-accuracy decomposition in anagram solving. They found little or no partial information: people could not give an accurate response before they finished. Earlier SAD work in other tasks always found partial information. Authors read it as a discrete, all-or-none shift at solution.
numbers: 2 experiments. No participant or accuracy numbers on the page.
quote: found little or no partial information in the anagram task
limits: Abstract only. A behavioural partial-information test, not a rating of nearness. It speaks against gradual accrual of solution knowledge in anagrams.
agent_relevance: Anagram-type problems may give no usable early signal. A rule that needs gradual evidence of nearing a solution can fail on such tasks; keep the count rule as the fallback.

source: Smith & Healy (1998) The time-course of the generation effect, Memory & Cognition 26, 135-142 (text about Smith & Kounios 1996)
finding: A read PDF that cites Smith & Kounios. SAD found slow growth of partial information in word recognition, recognition memory, semantic access and complex semantic relations. Smith and Kounios applied SAD to anagrams and found little or no partial information, suggesting one discrete shift. It also notes accurate metacognitive judgments for algebra problems (Metcalfe & Wiebe 1987).
numbers: No numbers for the anagram study itself.
limits: Secondary; confirms the result but adds no data. Still no source with anagram solvability-judgment numbers (Novick & Sherman 2003).
agent_relevance: Two human findings coexist: gradual warmth in algebra insight problems, all-or-none in anagrams. No single law of progress monitoring is supported.

source: Novick & Sherman (2003) On the nature of insight solutions: evidence from skill differences in anagram solution, QJEP 56A, 351-382
finding: Full text not reached. Only second-hand lines from search results: anagrams can give both insight-like and search-like solutions in expert solvers, and participants were screened with an anagram pretest (12 or more of 20 correct for the good group).
numbers: Screening cut-off 12/20 correct (from a later paper). No judgment data seen.
limits: Not opened. The focus-line claim that anagram solvability judgments improve with time is still UNSUPPORTED here.
agent_relevance: Do not cite anagram solvability numbers. Gap 3 stays open.

source: Harhen & Bornstein (2023) Overharvesting in human patch foraging reflects rational structure learning and adaptive planning, PNAS
finding: Humans and other foragers systematically stay in a patch too long ('overharvesting'), the opposite of leaving a promising line too early. The paper shows this follows from rational structure learning and uncertainty. In a patch-leaving task, human residence times adapted to the richness and dynamics of the environment as the model predicted.
numbers: 176 MTurk participants recruited; 60 excluded (36 residence-time outliers, 33 failed instruction quiz, 17 failed catch trials; criteria overlap), so about 116 kept.
limits: Foraging task, not problem solving. Human error direction is over-persistence, so a human analogue to LLM underthinking is weak.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: no human analogue to underthinking found. Humans err by staying too long. Thresholds for our trigger cannot be copied from human data; LLMs err in both directions.

source: Incubation and interactivity in insight problem solving (2020), Psychological Research (cheap necklace problem; cites Chu, Dewald & Chronicle 2007)
finding: Reports that solvers have been seen to persevere with the dead-end 'join the ends of the chains' strategy (Chu, Dewald and Chronicle 2007). The best fix mixed hints that stop the obvious first move with a colour cue. It reads this as perceptual chunking plus the criterion for satisfactory progress both causing impasse.
numbers: Necklace costs: wrong first move costs 5 and ends at 20; correct plan costs 6 plus 9.
limits: Secondary. No perseverance rate was read. Chu et al. 2007 not opened.
agent_relevance: Human insight failure is perseverance on a locally progressing path. Supports a trigger that fires despite apparent progress.

source: Nanda et al. (2026) Wink: Recovering from Misbehaviors in Coding Agents (Meta), prevalence and classifier
finding: Production study of coding agents. Misbehaviors occur in about 30% of trajectories. Infinite loops are 2.18% (Sonnet 4.5) and 3.59% (Opus 4.5) of trajectories; the rise is significant (p<0.00001) even as instruction following improved. Detection used LLM classifiers with a set bar of 80% precision, run every 5 steps.
numbers: Static set 42,920 trajectories; classifiers on 10% of daily traffic (8k trajectories). Overall prevalence about 29%. Loops 2.18% vs 3.59%. Tool-call failures 10.99% vs 11.08%.
limits: Closed production data, trajectory-level labels from an LLM classifier, no ground-truth false-trigger rate beyond the 80% precision target.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partial: loops are rare (2-4%) in real coding traces and newer models loop more. A count rule would fire on a small share of traces; most trouble is other types.

source: Nanda et al. (2026) Wink: intervention results and failure reasons (RQ1-RQ4)
finding: When a monitor sees a misbehavior and injects a nudge, 90.93% of single-intervention cases recover; multiple interventions recover 79.07%. In a shadow-mode test the misbehavior rate fell from 18.61% to 15.14% (p=0.00003). Live A/B: tokens per session -5.3%, engineer interventions -4.2%. Non-recovery reasons: agent ignored guidance 37%, premature termination 22%, tool failures 19%, merge conflicts 11%, false negatives 11%.
numbers: 10,554 intervened trajectories; judge precision 85.71%; shadow test 711 vs 759 trajectories; recovery causes: infinite loops 39%, replan reminder 26%, 'do not overdo' 17%, correct arguments 17%.
limits: Only one response type tested (guidance injected into the agent). No arm tried restart, ask or stop. Recovery judged by an LLM.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a nudge works, but responses were not compared. Warning: 37% of failures were the agent ignoring the instruction, so a trigger needs an enforced response.

source: OnTrack (2026) real-time monitoring and intervention in LLM agent trajectories (SWE-bench, 2,294 trajectories)
finding: Streaming monitor that detects loops, stalls and repeated tool calls without new results, and ranks early trajectories. Over the first 8 steps it ranked failing runs below succeeding ones better than content similarity (+0.057 AUROC; CI +0.033 to +0.080). An abort policy saved 17-18% of compute on failing runs at about 83% precision.
numbers: 2,294 SWE-agent trajectories; +0.057 AUROC at k=8; 17-18% compute saved on failed runs; precision about 83% (5 of 6 aborts correct); stops roughly one in four failing runs.
limits: Authors say rival stopping policies can match the savings at equal false-stop rates, and that simple loop/stall heuristics match or beat its recall on real traces. Reference set only 5 instances.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 5: simple loop/stall counts do about as well as the elaborate monitor on SWE traces. The elaborate part mainly buys a lower false-alarm operating point.

source: OnTrack (2026) limitations: false stops and task-generic signals
finding: Even with density thresholds the shipped operating point interrupts 13-21% of well-behaved traces. Reference-free variants flagged 29-32 of 40 benign traces, versus 13 of 40 for the full method. Length-controlled AUROC for predicting patch correctness was 0.526; every task-generic trajectory signal sat near chance.
numbers: Benign false alarms 13/40 (full) vs 29-32/40 (reference-free). Length-controlled AUROC 0.526 (cosine 0.540). Cost-limit failures detected at 0.979 AUROC.
limits: SWE-agent traces are homogeneous (search-read-edit-test). Authors expect different results on diverse tool workflows.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 answered for coding agents: a naive structure or repetition rule can flag a large share of normal traces (13-21% at the shipped point, 72-80% for the weakest variants). A trigger needs a priced cost for false stops.

source: DeLoop (2026): repeated actions as self-supervision for long-horizon agents
finding: Defines a loop as re-issuing a tool call and getting the same observation, a step with no new information. Loops are native to Qwen, Llama and Gemini agents and increase when history is compressed. Training on the agent's own loops as negatives cut loops sharply with similar success.
numbers: Qwen3-8B on CodeGym under compression: loops 57.3% -> 6.1%, about one third of the steps. Qwen3-32B success 37.7% -> 44.8%. Llama-3.1-8B loops 44.0% (full history) and 43.7% (compressed) -> 2.0%. Qwen3-14B loop rate 33.3% -> 42.9% and 32B 26.0% -> 38.5% under compression; success -8.9 and -9.0 points.
limits: CodeGym synthetic tasks, small models, a training method not a prompt rule. Loop = identical call and observation, a strict repeat test.
agent_relevance: A strict 'same call, same result' rule is well defined and loops are common (26-57%) when memory is compressed. Our own summary step may cause loops; an exact-repeat count is cheap and worth having.

source: Han et al. (2026) VLAA-GUI: knowing when to stop, recover and search (Loop Breaker ablation)
finding: A fixed count rule with escalation. Tier 1: same action with no visible change twice (threshold 2) forces a different interaction mode. Tier 2: same screen three times forces a different overall strategy. Tier 3: an external judge says keep or switch and the repeated action is blacklisted. Removing the Loop Breaker hurt a loop-prone backbone and did almost nothing for a strong one.
numbers: OSWorld, Gemini 3 Flash: full 63.14 (50 steps) and 68.77 (100 steps); without Loop Breaker 58.90 and 66.95. Sonnet 4.6: full 71.11 and 71.67; without 69.67 and 71.63. Windows Agent Arena full 61.0% vs 55.8% without Loop Breaker at 100 steps. Loop Breaker nearly halves wasted steps for loop-prone backbones.
limits: No comparison with a confidence-based trigger. Ablation is one run per cell; differences of 0.04 to 2 points are small. Thresholds fixed across tasks.
agent_relevance: Best controlled evidence for a code-set count rule with a forced strategy switch (gaps 1 and 6). The effect depends on how loop-prone the backbone is.

source: Judged Useless, Queried Anyway: tool-using agents rarely turn their own evidence judgments into stopping (2026)
finding: Seven agents judged a failing source's results useless 97-100% of the time, yet most rarely stopped on that judgment. Prompt cues (budget, a stated stopping rule, a call price) changed when they stopped but not what they stopped on. Only a harness-enforced rule that makes the agent answer after five consecutive useless results made stopping follow the evidence, raising failing-source success for every model. A pre-registered replication on 300 fresh questions confirmed it.
numbers: Enforced rule threshold = 5 consecutive useless judgments; stopping-sensitivity delta +0.33 to +0.40; success gain (mean6) +0.026 to +0.097 for four open models and Claude Haiku 4.5; non-inferior in 18 of 20 tests where the source works or recovers; combined with a budget non-inferior in 14 of 14 pre-registered tests; beats a random-timing signal by 0.011 to 0.029; unaided agents lose 6-13 points against the best fixed cap chosen in hindsight.
quote: Stopping follows the evidence only when the harness enforces an integration step
limits: Retrieval tasks with controlled source failures, mostly 7-8B open models plus Haiku 4.5. The 'useless' signal is easy to read here. An LLM-written running count placed in context did not help (delta -0.14 to -0.24 for three 7-8B models).
agent_relevance: Best answer to gaps 1 and 4: a code-enforced count of consecutive no-new-information judgments beats giving the model the information or a stated rule. The model's graded judgment is accurate but not acted on.

source: Judged Useless, Queried Anyway: backup tool, running count and cheap detector (same paper)
finding: Offering a backup search tool did not make leaving evidence-driven: unaided agents were no more likely to leave as useless results piled up (delta at most +0.02). Disabling the failing tool after five useless judgments did (+0.26 and +0.30 for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B). A cheap lexical detector (few shared content words) did about as well as the agent at flagging useless results.
numbers: By the fourth action Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B had switched on 17% and 49% of questions; Llama-3.1-8B success 0.05 vs 0.50 with a working primary tool. Doubling the budget gave the budget-cued 7-8B Qwen models 61-71% more calls for no gain.
limits: The lexical detector and running-count results are exploratory. Reasoning mode and larger models largely still fail to stop on evidence; only Claude Sonnet 5 partly does without prompting.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a forced switch (disable the failing tool) works where a prompt-level suggestion fails. The response must be enforced; the trigger can be a cheap proxy.

source: Wang et al. (2025) EAT: Entropy After </Think> for reasoning model early exiting: baselines
finding: A graded signal (entropy after a forced stop token) was compared with two cheaper rules across token budgets: a fixed token cap and a count of unique answers across K rollouts (#UA@K, a convergence count). EAT cut tokens 12-22% without hurting accuracy on MATH-500 and AIME-2025 (up to 21% on AIME-2025). #UA@K only worked for K at least 16 and cost many extra tokens.
numbers: Token cap swept 250 to 10,000 in steps of 250; #UA@K with K in {8,16,32}, threshold 1-3. #UA@K needs K>=16; rollouts dominate cost and run more than 50 times slower than EAT. EAT similar to a 5-token confidence score, rollout-free. Works with proxy models (1.5B for Llama-70B; 4B for Claude 3.7).
limits: Math/science only. Authors say EAT is not advantageous on single-turn tool calling. Not an open-ended agent trace.
agent_relevance: The one head-to-head found of a graded signal vs a fixed cap vs an answer-count rule at matched token use. The graded signal won, but the count rule is handicapped by needing rollouts; a repeat count over actions already in the trace costs nothing.

source: Cao et al. (2026) Metacognitive Harness: ablation of the controller (N=100)
finding: A learned controller on pre-solve (FOK) and post-solve (JOL) self-ratings beat the best hand-tuned confidence rule. Random retry at the same budget came close. Re-feeding the full previous reasoning to the retry hurt compared with compact feedback.
numbers: 100-question set, Sonnet-4.6, Pass@1 44.0, Oracle@4 53.0. Full harness 47.0 [37,57], avg K 2.58, early-stop hit 76.7%. Hand-tuned (1-JOL)*FOK rule 42.0 [32,52], K 2.40. Random retry same K 45.7. FOK only 42.0; JOL only 45.0. Full previous context 40.0, K 3.09. No prior state 45.0.
limits: Intervals overlap heavily (about 20 points wide). Differences of 1-5 points are not reliable. Ratings are per attempt, not mid-solve.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the only graded-vs-hand-rule comparison, at tiny N and with overlapping CIs; no count-rule arm. Gap 6: a compact summary beats re-feeding the failed trace.

source: Cao et al. (2026) Metacognitive Harness: within-problem resolution and Table 5 re-read
finding: Self-rated confidence (JOL) varies little across attempts at the same problem: median within-problem SD 0.048, versus SD 0.270 across problems (5.6 times wider). So it ranks problems but not attempts. Re-read of Table 5 (LiveCodeBench v6): Pass@1 74.3 to harness 84.3 (+10.0), avg K 2.6, cost $0.56 vs $0.94 for the aggregator at 83.4.
numbers: Within SD 0.048 vs across 0.270. Table 5: Self-Refine 80.6; Budget Forcing 80.0; Verifier Reranking 78.9; Aggregator 83.4; Harness 84.3 (oracle 86.0). Table 4 (HLE-Verified): 48.0 to 60.0, K 1.4, cost $0.98.
limits: The +10.0 is the overall LiveCodeBench figure, confirmed from Table 5 text; Hard/Easy splits were not found in the text read. Confidence is taken after each attempt, not during one.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: within one solve the graded rating carries little signal. Use it to decide how much effort a problem deserves, not to detect stalls inside one attempt.

source: Ruan et al. (2026) Doomed from the Start: early abort of LLM agent episodes via a recall-controlled probe cascade
finding: Hidden-state probes predict eventual agent failure from the first interaction rounds, earlier than monitors using only visible behaviour. A cascade of per-round gates holds recall of successful episodes at a user target, so the false-abort rate is controlled by design. Behaviour-only monitoring was consistently weaker.
numbers: TextCraft and WebShop, three small models. Token cuts at 90% recall: up to 60.2% (TextCraft) and 54.9% (WebShop); at 95% recall 45.0% and 41.5%. Probe AUC 0.86 and 0.81 at round 1 for two TextCraft models; WebShop Qwen3-1.7B 0.591 at round 1 to 0.896 at round 3. Behaviour-only saving 9.9% vs 41.6% probe (WebShop Qwen3-1.7B), 24.8% vs 42.2% (TextCraft Qwen-2.5-7B). ALFWorld: 477 rollouts, AUC 0.815, saves 10.7% vs 3.3%.
limits: Needs open-weight hidden states; small models; two game-like environments. Does not test a repeat-count rule.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: an external, non-self-report signal can be informative early and its false-abort rate can be set. Not available for a closed-API agent; for us only visible signals apply, and those were weaker here.

source: d'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models: spontaneous mid-reasoning shifts
finding: Mid-trace 'Aha' shifts in reasoning models are rare and usually do not help. Traces with a shift were much less accurate than traces without. The shift is a sign of unstable inference, not of insight. So the text-level analogue of the human abrupt signal does not predict success.
numbers: Over 1M traces; Qwen2.5-1.5B pooled N=723,200: shifts about 6.31% of samples; accuracy 2.57% with a shift vs 16.44% without. GPT-4o shift rate 0.88-2.21%, DeepSeek-R1 0.00-0.25% on MATH-500. In Math, shifts cost -22.88 points in low-entropy traces and -7.40 in high-entropy traces.
limits: A behavioural cue detector, not a warmth rating. Mostly GRPO-tuned small models; math, crosswords, Rush Hour.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partial: no study elicits warmth ratings mid-solve, but shifts detected in text do not predict success. Do not use 'sudden change of approach' text as a progress signal.

source: d'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) forced reconsideration under high entropy
finding: Appending a reconsideration cue and sampling a second pass improved accuracy on Math, with larger gains where entropy was high. In Crosswords the net gain was small.
numbers: Math accuracy 0.3221 to 0.4062 (+8.41 pp), 50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong. Crosswords 0.0970 to 0.1015 (+0.45 pp; 5,380 vs 5,004). Rush Hour +0.01 pp at near-zero base.
limits: Second sample at doubled cost; not compared with simply sampling twice. Math results come from small tuned models.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partial: an externally triggered second pass, gated by uncertainty, helps on math. A restart-style response was measured, but not against switch-strategy or ask.

source: Reasoning Theater (2026): disentangling model beliefs from chain-of-thought
finding: Activation probes can decode a reasoning model's final answer far earlier than a text monitor can, especially on easy recall questions (performative reasoning). Backtracking and 'aha' points occur almost only where probes show large belief shifts, so they track real uncertainty. Probe-guided early exit cut tokens with similar accuracy.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 671B and GPT-OSS 120B. Token cuts up to 80% on MMLU and 30% on GPQA-Diamond.
limits: Needs activations. A text monitor on the visible chain of thought is much weaker on easy items.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partial: an internal belief trajectory exists, but a text-level read of it is poor. A warmth-style prompt may measure a performance, not a state.

source: Gai et al. (2026) Understanding and mitigating premature confidence for better LLM reasoning (CMU)
finding: How confidence evolves during reasoning predicts flawed reasoning: committing to an answer early and then rationalising it ('premature confidence'). Training that rewards gradual confidence growth and penalises early commitment improved accuracy. The only study found that treats a graded within-solve confidence curve as a quality signal; the LLM counterpart of gradual warmth.
numbers: Countdown accuracy 3.2x (+42.0 pp), flawed reasoning down 48 pp; AIME Pass@64 +6.6 pp; models 1.5B to 8B. Gains grow with model size and task difficulty.
limits: Abstract read only. Trained with RL, not prompted; the shaping objective changes the model rather than gating a scaffold.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partial: gradual confidence matters, but no warmth rating was elicited from a frozen model. A scaffold cannot train; the practical reading is that a jump to certainty early in a solve is a risk flag.

source: ReTRAIL (2026): retrospective exploration and evolving for long-horizon agents
finding: Simply giving existing agents a rewind operation gave mixed results and could lower performance. A trained policy that rewinds from unproductive states and carries lessons from abandoned branches gained on all four benchmarks, and reflection-guided retries gave the biggest gains.
numbers: MineSweeper: 58.8% without rewind, 63.5% with proactive rewind, 95.3% with up to 3 reflection-guided attempts vs 70.8% strongest baseline. T@3 beats best baseline by 24.5 pp (MineSweeper) and 10.2 (ScienceWorld). T@4: 97.8% (MineSweeper), 95.1% (Sokoban). Within-attempt gains 1.3 (ALFWorld) to 10.9 (Sokoban) points.
limits: Trained policy on four game-like environments, not a prompt-only scaffold. The rewind is an environment feature.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a bare restart or rewind can hurt; restart plus carried-forward lessons helps. Do not make the response to a trigger a bare restart.

source: Real-Time Detection and Repair of LLM Agent Failures (2026): telemetry monitors with CUSUM alarms
finding: Cheap monitors on step telemetry (embeddings, token uncertainty, action metadata) trained on healthy runs. They work on injected failures but transfer weakly to organic ones. A completion check caught omissions (7 of 7 silent aborts) but monitors caught 1 of 3 organic fabrications and ranked the organic set at or below chance without recalibration.
numbers: 2,823 episodes, three frameworks, qwen2.5 7b/3b, llama3.1 8b, gemini-2.5-flash. Content-grounding channel lifted content detection 0.28 to 0.59 (+0.31). Fabrication study underpowered: 2 hallucinations in 55 pre-registered episodes, 9 across 175 organic episodes.
limits: Abstract only read. Organic sample small. Failure types differ from stalls.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: detectors tuned on injected faults overstate performance on organic ones. Test any trigger on real traces from our own agent.

source: SmartSwitch (2025): overcoming underthinking by promoting deeper thought exploration
finding: Detects when a long-CoT model switches thought too soon, scores the abandoned thought with a process reward model, and if it looked promising backtracks and inserts a 'deepening prompt'. An LLM-side answer to leaving a promising line too early.
numbers: In the example from DeepSeek-R1 the response had 74 different thoughts of about 150 tokens each. No accuracy numbers read (abstract and figure caption only).
limits: Math benchmarks only; abstract-level read, so gains were not checked.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: underthinking is a documented LLM failure with a monitor-and-backtrack fix, but no human analogue was found. The trigger should not fire on every switch of thought.

source: Negative search result: direct re-test of the Hedne et al. (2016) warmth design; LLM warmth elicitation mid-solve
finding: Searches of Europe PMC and a paper-search API for warmth, feeling of warmth and progress-rating studies found no direct re-test of the 100% confidence criterion or the 40-vs-5 ratings design, and no LLM study that asks a model for warmth ratings mid-solve and checks whether they rise before success. Recent Aha-rating papers (Wiley & Miller 2026; Chandolia 2026; Doulfoukar 2026) cite Hedne but do not re-run it.
numbers: None. Full texts of three 2026 Aha papers mention Hedne only in citations or one line on Metcalfe & Wiebe's warmth ratings.
limits: Absence of evidence only. The shared web-search budget was used up, and arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate limited.
agent_relevance: Gaps 8 and 9 stay open. Cite as 'none found', not 'none exists'.
